text.p: Goblins are small, black-hearted, selfish humanoids that lair in caves, abandoned mines, despoiled dungeons, and other dismal settings. Individually weak, goblins gather in large-sometimes overwhelming-numbers. They crave power and regularly abuse whatever authority they obtain.

Goblinoids. Goblins belong to a family of creatures called goblinoids. Their larger cousins, hobgoblins and bugbears, like to bully goblins into submission. Goblins are lazy and undisciplined, making them poor servants, laborers, and guards.

Malicious Glee. Motivated by greed and malice, goblins can't help but celebrate the few times they have the upper hand. They dance, caper with sheer joy when victory is theirs. Once their revels have ended, goblins delight in the torment of other creatures and embrace all manner of wickedness.

Leaders and Followers. Goblins are ruled by the strongest or smartest among them. A goblin boss might command a single lair, while a goblin king or queen (who is nothing more than a glorified goblin boss) rules hundreds of goblins, spread out among multiple lairs to ensure the tribe's survival. Goblin bosses are easily ousted, and many goblin tribes are taken over by hobgoblin warlords or bugbear chiefs.

Challenging Lairs. Goblins festoon their lairs with alarms designed to signal the arrival of intruders. Those lairs are also riddled with narrow tunnels and bolt-holes that human-sized creatures can't navigate, but which goblins can crawl through with ease, allowing them to flee or to circle around and surprise their enemies. Rat Keepers and Wolf Riders. Goblins have an affinity for rats and wolves, raising them to serve as companions and mounts, respectively. Like rats, goblins shun sunlight and sleep underground during the day. Like wolves, they are pack hunters, made bolder by their numbers. When they hunt from the backs of wolves, goblins use hit-and-run attacks.

Worshipers of Maglubiyet. Maglubiyet the Mighty One, the Lord of Depths and Darkness, is the greater god of goblinoids. Envisioned by most goblins as an eleven-foot-tall battle-scarred goblin with black skin and fire erupting from his eyes, he is worshiped not out of adoration but fear. Goblins believe that when they die in battle, their spirits join the ranks of Maglubiyet's army on the plane of Acheron. This is a "privilege" that most goblins dread, fearing the Mighty One's eternal tyranny even more than death.

id-00001.desc: The goblin can take the Disengage or Hide action as a bonus action on each of its turns.
id-00001.name: Nimble Escape

linklist.link: Book - D&D Dragon of Icespire Peak
Story: Episode#0.01.00 Dragon of Icespire Peak Overview

text.p: “The inn is thick with anxious voices, but one name rises again and again—Adabra Gwynn. She’s the herbalist who lives alone at Umbrage Hill, a few hours south of town. She’s the only one in miles who can brew healing draughts, and with the caravan’s potions lost, Phandalin’s survival depends on her. But Umbrage Hill is dangerous. A beast’s shadow has been seen circling the skies above it, and folk whisper that no one should travel there alone. The townsfolk plead for someone to reach her, to bring her back or at least make sure she’s safe. All eyes turn to you. If Adabra falls, Phandalin falls with her.”

p.b: If Kaelen is in the Party

text.frame: “As the townsfolk murmur about Adabra Gwynn, a few eyes flick toward your quiet companion—the wood elf with the hunter’s gaze. Kaelen has stood apart through most of the noise, watchful as ever, his expression unreadable. When the room settles, he finally speaks, his voice low and steady. ‘If the herbalist is the one who keeps Phandalin supplied with healing draughts… then she’s the one we cannot afford to lose. We should go. Now.’ The words are simple, but the intent is clear. Kaelen says no more, returning to silence, but his hand lingers on his bow as if to underscore his point.” Perfect — you’re setting up Umbrage Hill with tension, mystery, and a great first use of Kaelen whether he’s in the group or a character they meet on the road. I’ll clean this into a structured Journey Scene you can run either way.

list.li: Distance: ~2 hours on foot.
Terrain: Light rolling hills, open grassland, patches of rocky ground.
Mood: The sky hangs heavy, the memory of the dragon’s earlier roar still fresh in the party’s minds.

text.frame: “An hour into your hike, the air shudders with a deafening roar. It rumbles across the plains from the southeast—the very direction of Umbrage Hill. Birds scatter from the grasses, and for a heartbeat, the land falls silent as though even the earth is holding its breath.”

p.b: If Kaelen is in the Party

list.li: Kaelen immediately raises a hand, halting the group.
He kneels, eyes narrowing as he listens to the sound fade into the distance.

text.frame: “Hold. That was no echo of the mountains. Something hunts ahead.”

list.li: Perception DC 12 → Estimate distance (several miles off, not directly on them).
History or Nature DC 15 → Recognize the roar type, but players must guess what beast it belongs to.
Natural 20 on above → They recall tales of a manticore’s bellow.

p.b: If Kaelen is Not in the Party

text.frame: “Moments later, you spot movement ahead—a lone wood elf crouched low, his fingers tracing faint impressions in the dirt. A longbow rests at his side, and his cloak blends into the grasses as if he’s grown from the wild itself.”

list.li: The elf straightens, brushing dust from his hands. His gaze is sharp but not hostile.
‘Tracks,’ he says simply. ‘Someone I’m searching for passed this way. I’ve no time for conversation.’
Kaelen’s eyes harden. He shoulders his bow and melts back into the grasses, gone before you can take another step.
This establishes Kaelen as wary, focused, and driven — a figure who could be ally or stranger, depending on how the party treats him

text.frame: “The windmill of Umbrage Hill rises above the grassy plain, its blades creaking slowly in the breeze. The path bends toward it when a sudden scream rips through the air, followed by the echoing roar of something massive. From the hilltop, a terrified commoner bolts out of the mill’s doorway, sprinting downhill, his face twisted in terror. Above him, a hulking silhouette takes shape against the sky—a monstrous beast with the body of a lion, enormous bat-like wings, and a barbed tail lashing in the air. With a roar, it surges forward, claws outstretched, flying straight for the fleeing commoner. At the same time, another roar thunders from the hilltop. A second creature, its tail slamming against the stone, claws and wings battering the shutters, is savaging the windmill itself—trying to tear its way inside.”

list.li: If successful, the flying manticore is distracted long enough for the commoner to dive out of its reach and survive.
If failed, the manticore rends the fleeing man before the party’s eyes. His screams are silenced in an instant.

text.p: This gives the players agency: save a life or watch the horror unfold.

id-00028.name: Episode#0.01.00 Dragon of Icespire Peak Overview

linklist.link: Book - D&D Dragon of Icespire Peak

text.frame: “The frontier of Phandalin lies under a gathering shadow. From the peaks of the Sword Mountains, a dragon has descended—its wings scattering beasts, its presence driving monsters into new lairs. With each passing day, the land grows more dangerous. Farms are abandoned, trade routes falter, and rumors of fiery breath and frozen death spread like wildfire. In the wake of this upheaval, the orc tribes have grown restless. Some now march under the guidance of half-orc shamans who gather during stormy nights to perform dark rituals to their storm god. Their rites call down lightning and thunder, and whispers tell of a primal beast loosed upon the plains, thundering across the frontier at their command. Even the dark canopy of Neverwinter Wood is no refuge. When storms roll in, strange lights flicker between the trees, and the cries of unseen things echo through the branches. From the wilds and mountains to the very outskirts of Phandalin itself, danger presses in on all sides. The town has turned to outsiders—adventurers, mercenaries, and would-be heroes. Coin and glory await those bold enough to face the frontier, but so too does a rising storm. This is where your paths cross, and where your story begins.”
text.h: Scene 1: Caravan on the Triboar Trail
text.frame: “The wheels of the caravan creak and groan as it rolls along the rutted Triboar Trail, the late afternoon sun casting long shadows across the fields. To your south, beyond rolling hills, lies the frontier town of Phandalin—the destination of weary travelers, wandering adventurers, and hopeful settlers. Around you, other wagons rumble forward, the sound of hooves and murmured voices carrying in the summer air. This is your moment to introduce yourselves—what do the others see as you travel together toward Phandalin?”

list.li: Let the players roleplay their introductions and reasons for heading to Phandalin.

text.frame: “As the caravan crests a low rise, the driver calls out and turns south onto a smaller trail. There, nestled against the foothills of the Sword Mountains, lies Phandalin—a scattering of stone cottages, wooden homes, and farmland carved from wilderness. It looks quiet, almost peaceful.”

“A sudden, bone-shaking roar splits the air. From the east, the shadow of vast wings sweeps over the trail. A white dragon bursts from the clouds, diving low, its scales flashing like shards of ice in the sunlight. Its cry sends livestock scattering and sets the caravan horses into a panic.” The beast swoops over the wagons, its icy breath blasting across crates of supplies, freezing wood and shattering glass. Livestock scatter into the fields, and settlers scream as the shadow of wings circles overhead. The dragon lashes out at stragglers, tearing into wagons, its tail smashing wood to splinters. If you stand to fight, its wings buffet you, knocking you to the dirt. If you flee, its icy roar chills you to the bone as it hunts the weak and slow. It is a predator, and you are prey.”*
text.p: Cryovain doesn’t fight to kill here—this is a cinematic “you can’t win” encounter:

list.li: Anyone who tries to fight is knocked away by tail swipes, wing gusts, or claws (non-lethal).
Anyone who flees is chased down and eaten by Cryovain—showing the dragon’s lethality without touching PCs.
The caravan leader yells at the PCs to run: “You fools! Run! Get to Phandalin!”

text.frame: “At last, with a triumphant cry, the dragon beats its wings and veers westward, leaving ruin in its wake. The air falls silent, broken only by the sobs of survivors and the panicked whinnies of scattered horses.”

list.li: PCs are forced to run for the safety of the town.
Cryovain doesn’t pursue them directly—he is more interested in terrorizing and feasting on the caravan stragglers.
The party escapes into Phandalin as chaos begins spreading about “the dragon sighting.”

text.frame: “Your lungs burn as you flee the trail, stumbling into the safety of Phandalin. The dragon’s roar fades into the distance, and the townsfolk cautiously emerge from doorways and shutters, faces pale and fearful. Though the dragon doesn’t strike at the town itself, its shadow lingers long in their eyes. A tall, black-scaled dragonborn in a weathered cloak stands in the center of it all, his amber eyes sweeping the scene. You recognize him as the same figure who urged you to run for your lives on the road. He raises a clawed hand and gestures toward the timber-framed inn. ‘Inside, quickly! Rest your feet and your spirits—you’re safe, for now.’”*

list.li: The PCs are guided into Toblen Stonehill’s inn (your image).
Toblen is shaken but hospitable, offering the survivors refuge and a warm hearth.
Immediate Action: He makes sure the party gets inside Stonehill Inn, checks their condition, and reassures them.
Tone: Calm, authoritative, like a veteran who has done this before.
Personality: Uses short, steady phrases to steady the party, mentor-like.

text.frame: “The inn fills with anxious voices. Survivors argue over what remains of the caravan, merchants clutch ledgers in despair, and families sob for those lost on the road. Outside, the streets buzz with fearful talk—the dragon’s roar is on every tongue. The truth is plain: much of the shipment is ruined. Crates of food lie frozen and shattered, health potions scattered in the mud. Without them, miners will suffer, the harvest will falter, and the town’s lifeline is cut thin. ‘The potions were for the mines!’ one merchant cries. ‘Without them, sickness will claim us!’ ‘The fields won’t last without those tools!’ a farmer shouts, fear in his eyes. A caravan guard slams his fist on the table. ‘Half my men are gone, and for what? The dragon’s still out there!’ At last, the dragonborn speaks, his voice steady amid the chaos. He looks to you and says: ‘You saw it with your own eyes. This town won’t last without help. The board will tell you where you’re needed most—but make no mistake. The storm has already broken. Choose your stand.’”

list.li: If the party wanders: Blacktide doesn’t force them; he lets them breathe, but checks in later.
He might approach them in the street or at the inn with a lead: “I heard talk near the Townmaster’s Hall. If you’ve steel enough left in your bones, there’s coin to be had and good you might do.”

p.b: 2. Seeking Quests / Finding the Job Board

list.li: If they find the board first: let the board do the work.
Blacktide will still show up, either confirming what they’ve found or filling in context: “You’ve sharp eyes. Those notices tell half the tale—the rest you’ll hear from the folk who posted them.”

p.b: 3. If They Stall / Don’t Know Where to Go

list.li: Blacktide acts as the gentle nudge, presenting the first quest in-character so momentum never stalls.

linklist.link: Book - D&D Dragon of Icespire Peak

text.frame: “The Stonehill Inn is a modest, two-story roadhouse with the warm smell of stew and wood smoke drifting from its common room. The floorboards creak under the weight of weary travelers, and lantern light flickers across the walls. Laughter and whispers mix with the clink of mugs, though tonight, the air carries unease after the dragon’s roar. A friendly, broad-shouldered man behind the bar offers a reassuring smile to every patron who enters.”

list.li: Appearance: A short, stocky man in his 30s with sun-darkened skin, cropped brown hair, and a quick, friendly grin. He wears a simple apron over travel-worn clothes.
Personality: Jovial, optimistic, and quick to trust newcomers. Always trying to make strangers feel welcome.

Hook: He came to Phandalin chasing gold in the mines, but soon realized he was better suited to running an inn. He enjoys hearing tales from travelers and quietly worries about how long Phandalin can survive the growing dangers.

text.h: Session AAR (After-Action Review) — GM Guide & Instructions=
text.p: At the end of each session, you may choose or roll which questions to ask.

list.li: Per category: roll 1d10 to select one question (reroll duplicates), or hand-pick 1–3.
Pacing: Aim for 10–12 minutes total. Ask 1–2 questions from 3–5 categories.
Format tips: Let players answer in any order, invite one “+1/agree” per comment, and capture 1 actionable takeaway before closing.

text.p: 1. Pick/Roll 3–5 questions across categories (1d10 per chosen category).
2. Round-Robin answers (30–60s each); allow one “+1” per comment.
3. Capture 2 wins + 1 fix for next session (write it down).
4. Confirm: Any blockers or wishlist items before we close?
1. What story beat landed best for you tonight, and why did it work?
2. Where did the pacing drag, and what would have sped it up for you?
3. Which hook or mystery are you most curious to chase next?
4. Did any scene feel rushed or undercooked? What would you add?
5. Which choice or consequence felt most meaningful this session?
6. Was there a moment you wished for more spotlight or setup?
7. Name a tone/mood that worked (e.g., tense, heroic, eerie). Where did we hit it?
8. Did the session length feel right? If not, where would you trim or expand?
9. What narrative payoff felt earned (or not yet earned)?
10. If we replayed one scene, what would you change to improve flow?
1. Which combat moment felt most exciting and why?
2. Did the difficulty feel right? What would make it better next time?
3. Was there a tactical option you wanted but couldn’t use?
4. Did any ability or build feel invalidated or overshadowed?
5. How did the action economy feel (too many/few enemies, turn speed)?
6. What made positioning/terrain interesting—or not?
7. Did loot, resources, or attrition feel rewarding vs. punishing?
8. Was rules clarity an issue at any point? Which rule needs a quick table note?
9. Which monster/NPC tactic felt smart, fair, or cheesy?
10. If you could add one combat twist (environment, objective, timer), what is it?
1. Which NPC was most memorable, and what made them pop?
2. Did you feel you had enough chances to roleplay your character’s voice?
3. Which interaction (ally, rival, merchant, faction) felt most engaging?
4. Was any motivation unclear (yours or an NPC’s)? What clarity would help?
5. Name a character bond/flag you want the world to hit more often.
6. Did social stakes feel real? Where could they be raised?
7. Any dialogue beats you’d trim or tighten for momentum?
8. Which faction/organization do you want more screen time with—and how?
9. Did disguises, deception, or persuasion feel fairly adjudicated?
10. What callback to past events would’ve heightened a scene?
1. Which location detail (map, hazard, lore) pulled you in?
2. Did you feel agency in choosing where to go/what to do?
3. Was information discoverable at the right depth (clues, handouts, checks)?
4. Any travel/downtime moment that felt like filler? How to make it pay off?
5. Which mystery/environmental puzzle worked—or needed one more clue?
6. How did resource tracking (time, torches, spell slots) feel—tense or tedious?
7. What worldbuilding thread should we spotlight next session?
8. Did maps/props help you visualize, or do you want a different style?
9. Any procedural step (random encounter, hex, exploration action) to streamline?
10. What secret or vista would make exploration feel more “wow”?
1. What tool (Fantasy Grounds, VTT, dice, initiative method) sped things up?
2. What tool/process slowed us down, and how would you tweak it?
3. Was table time balanced? Anyone need more spotlight or shorter turns?
4. Did audio/music/SFX help or distract? What mix works best?
5. Any house rule to document on a 1-page cheat for quick reference?
6. Were status/effect tracking and conditions clear?
7. Did the recap + goals at start help you focus? What should that include?
8. How was communication (cross-talk, sidebars, clarity)? One fix?
9. Was scheduling/energy right for you? Prefer a break or tighter cadence?
10. What is one quality-of-life change we can try next session?
1. Safety Tools (Pause / Fade to Black / Step Away)
2. Consent & Boundaries
3. Table Expectations
4. PvP, Theft, and Party Conflict
5. Aftercare & Feedback
6. Current Lines & Veils (Living List)
SAFETY TOOLS (PAUSE / FADE TO BLACK / STEP AWAY)
Your comfort matters more than the scene. You never need to explain why.
PAUSE

list.li: Stop immediately. We will pause the scene and adjust.

text.p: FADE TO BLACK

list.li: We skip details and move forward.

text.p: STEP AWAY

list.li: Anyone may take a break at any time. No questions asked.

text.p: HOW TO USE THESE TOOLS

list.li: Say it out loud, type it in chat, or message the DM privately.
When a safety tool is used, we will course-correct quickly and continue.

text.p: This is a collaborative game. We protect each other’s comfort and keep the table enjoyable.

list.li: If something is not working for you, say PAUSE or message the DM.
Boundaries are respected immediately. No debate, no pushback.
If a topic is not listed, it can still be a boundary. Just tell the DM.
Sexual content: FADE TO BLACK
Torture/abuse detail: ALLOWED ON-SCREEN
Harm to children: NOT DEPICTED ON-SCREEN
If a player requests a new boundary (line or veil), the DM will add it to the Current Lines & Veils entry so everyone knows what is in effect.

text.p: To keep the game smooth, welcoming, and fun:

list.li: Be respectful. No harassment, slurs, or bullying.
Share the spotlight. Avoid talking over others; let people finish.
Play in good faith. We are here to create a great story together.
Keep the pace. Be ready on your turn; we will keep the game moving.
The DM may make a quick ruling to keep play moving.
If needed, we can review the ruling after the session.

text.p: Party conflict can be fun, but only with consent.

list.li: PvP is OFF by default.
No stealing from party members, sabotaging plans, or secret betrayal unless all involved players consent.
“It’s what my character would do” is never an excuse to ruin play.

text.p: If you want PC conflict, talk to the DM first so it stays fun and respectful.
We want the table to stay healthy over time.

list.li: At the end of sessions, we may do Stars & Wishes (highlights + what you want more of).
You can message the DM privately at any time (before, during, or after session).
If something felt off, the DM will address it discreetly and promptly.

text.p: This entry will be updated as players request boundaries.
LINES (NOT INCLUDED)
None listed yet
VEILS (FADE TO BLACK / MINIMAL DETAIL)
Sexual content (default)
ON-SCREEN ALLOWED BY DEFAULT (ADJUSTABLE ON REQUEST)
Torture/abuse detail
Use whichever feels best:

list.li: WASD: smooth pan
Middle Mouse Button: click-drag to pan
Spacebar + Left Click: click-drag to pan
Arrow Keys (no token selected): pan the view one grid at a time
Mouse wheel: zoom in/out
C / X keys: zoom in/out

text.p: With your token selected, Arrow Keys may move/nudge your token (if allowed).
If tokens are locked:

list.li: Primary move: Press ALT + click-drag from your token to show where you want to go (GM will approve/adjust).
Secondary move (multiple moves): Press CTRL + click-drag to place a second move after your primary move.
Shift + mouse wheel: rotate token
Ctrl + mouse wheel: resize token
Alt + mouse wheel: change altitude

text.p: Spacebar + double-click on the map to create a ping
Hold both mouse buttons to draw:
Arrow: both mouse buttons
Box: Shift + both mouse buttons
Circle: Ctrl + both mouse buttons
Cone: Alt + both mouse buttons
Right-click on the map to access Drawing Tools and Shapes.
Keep the Combat Tracker open during fights. It is the main hub for turn order and effects.
1. Confirm it is your turn in the Combat Tracker
2. Move (if needed)
3. Take your Action
4. Take a Bonus Action (if you have one)
5. Speak up if you have a Reaction trigger
1. Target the creature (see Targeting & Untargeting)
2. Click your attack on your character sheet (usually Actions/Combat)
3. Roll damage when prompted or when the DM asks for it
1. Target if needed, or tell the DM where you are placing an area effect
2. Cast from your Spells tab (or Actions if set up)
3. If saves are required, the DM may run them from the Combat Tracker

list.li: Tell the DM when you start concentration
If you take damage while concentrating, tell the DM so you can roll a concentration check

text.p: CONDITIONS & EFFECTS

list.li: Buffs, debuffs, and conditions may appear as Effects in the Combat Tracker.
If you think an effect should be added or removed, say so immediately.

text.p: PACE TIP
If you are unsure how to do something in FGU, say your intent out loud. The DM can keep things moving and help you after the moment.
Targeting tells Fantasy Grounds who you are attacking or affecting.
1. Select your character token
2. Hold CTRL and left-click the creature you want to target

list.li: With your token selected, hold CTRL and left-click the targeted creature again.
Use the Clear Targets button on the map to remove all targets at once.
You can also set targets in the Combat Tracker using the targeting controls/columns (when available).
This can be helpful when tokens overlap or the map is crowded.

text.p: TIP

The Action Time Tracker is a tool for Dungeon Masters to manage in-game time during exploration, downtime, and travel without tracking every second.
It divides player actions into four tiers based on the scale of the activity. Each tier has a default time increment and an optional dice roll to add uncertainty or tension.
This system helps:

list.li: Keep exploration pacing realistic
Make time feel meaningful (torches burn, spells expire, guards rotate shifts)
Avoid tedious micromanagement

text.p: 1. When players declare an action, the DM assigns it to one of four tiers based on its complexity and duration.
2. Either:

list.li: Use the default time for that tier (fast & simple), or
Roll the optional dice for more dynamic time progression.

text.p: 3. Advance the in-game clock accordingly.
text.frame: /roll d6
/roll 5d4
/roll 2d20+20
/roll 2d4

text.h: Step 1: Roll on Your Forecast Table
text.p: Your forecast table includes categories like:

list.li: Time
Sky
Precipitation
Thunderstorm
Wind
Cardinal Direction
Temperature
Tremors

text.p: Note: Each forecast element may be tagged as a trigger source for a specific cult (e.g., Cold Day = Air/Water Minor Hazard).
text.h: Step 2: Determine If a Hazard Event Is Triggered
text.p: Major hazards take priority followed by minor hazards. If multiple hazards trigger then decided with a d4. Once a major or minor hazard is decided roll on the appropriate Hazard Tier Table. If no hazard is rolled then fill in the fields:
Choose travel type (On Foot, Ground Mount, Ground Vehicle, Flying Mount).

list.li: Assign the base MP pool for that type.
If using Slow or Fast pace, adjust:
Slow pace = -25% MP
Fast pace = +25% MP (but anything beyond the Normal pace threshold requires forced march saves).

text.h: Step 2. Apply Terrain Cost per Hex

list.li: Each hex has a terrain type with a set MP cost.
Subtract that cost from the daily MP pool when the party enters the hex.
If the pool runs out mid-hex, note fractional progress (½ or ⅓). They finish the remainder next day.

text.p: Multiply hex costs by weather/environmental effects:

list.li: Rain = ×1.25
Storm/Blizzard = ×1.5
Extreme hazard (flood, gale, deep snow) = ×2

text.p: Apply additional modifiers for load, encumbrance, or mount fatigue if relevant.

list.li: Deduct MP until the pool is empty.
Record how many hexes were fully crossed.
If MP runs out inside a hex, note where they camp (½ or ⅓ through).
If the party uses Fast pace or attempts to push beyond their Normal MP pool, each extra hex requires saves:
CON Save DC 10 +2 per extra hex (for PCs and mounts).
Failure = gain 1 level of exhaustion (mounts become fatigued and can’t be pushed the following day).
After a long rest, MP pool resets to the base value.
If exhaustion or mount fatigue is present, reduce MP pool at DM’s discretion (e.g., –1 MP until recovered).

text.p: Social XP rewards players for roleplay, persuasion, negotiation, and creative interaction.
It ensures that talking, convincing, and roleplaying are just as rewarding as combat or exploration.
When a player makes a social roll (Persuasion, Deception, Intimidation, etc.), the DM assigns a Score (1–20).
Award XP to the roller based on the score and tier (see XP Matrix).
Helpers (any players who actively contributed or aided) each gain 10% of the roller’s XP award.
Example: A bard rolls Persuasion in Tier 2, Score 15 → 450 XP to the bard. Two helpers each gain 45 XP.

list.li: Roller: Gets the full XP shown.
Helpers: Each gets 10% of the roller’s XP.
XP is not split across the party — it’s awarded per player.

text.p: If the party resolves the encounter without any dice rolls (through pure roleplay or convincing argument):
Every player who actively participated in the conversation earns XP from the No-Roll Awards table.
Players who did not contribute do not earn this XP.
Example: In Tier 1, three players talk their way into gaining an audience with the duke without rolling. Each of those players gains 150 XP.

list.li: All players who actively roleplayed in the scene receive the XP.
Non-participants do not gain XP.
Roller → full XP.
Helpers → 10% each.
No-roll success → all participating players get Success/Exceptional XP.

text.h: Session AAR (After-Action Review) — GM Guide & Instructions=
text.p: At the end of each session, you may choose or roll which questions to ask.

list.li: Per category: roll 1d10 to select one question (reroll duplicates), or hand-pick 1–3.
Pacing: Aim for 10–12 minutes total. Ask 1–2 questions from 3–5 categories.
Format tips: Let players answer in any order, invite one “+1/agree” per comment, and capture 1 actionable takeaway before closing.

text.p: 1. Pick/Roll 3–5 questions across categories (1d10 per chosen category).
2. Round-Robin answers (30–60s each); allow one “+1” per comment.
3. Capture 2 wins + 1 fix for next session (write it down).
4. Confirm: Any blockers or wishlist items before we close?
1. What story beat landed best for you tonight, and why did it work?
2. Where did the pacing drag, and what would have sped it up for you?
3. Which hook or mystery are you most curious to chase next?
4. Did any scene feel rushed or undercooked? What would you add?
5. Which choice or consequence felt most meaningful this session?
6. Was there a moment you wished for more spotlight or setup?
7. Name a tone/mood that worked (e.g., tense, heroic, eerie). Where did we hit it?
8. Did the session length feel right? If not, where would you trim or expand?
9. What narrative payoff felt earned (or not yet earned)?
10. If we replayed one scene, what would you change to improve flow?
1. Which combat moment felt most exciting and why?
2. Did the difficulty feel right? What would make it better next time?
3. Was there a tactical option you wanted but couldn’t use?
4. Did any ability or build feel invalidated or overshadowed?
5. How did the action economy feel (too many/few enemies, turn speed)?
6. What made positioning/terrain interesting—or not?
7. Did loot, resources, or attrition feel rewarding vs. punishing?
8. Was rules clarity an issue at any point? Which rule needs a quick table note?
9. Which monster/NPC tactic felt smart, fair, or cheesy?
10. If you could add one combat twist (environment, objective, timer), what is it?
1. Which NPC was most memorable, and what made them pop?
2. Did you feel you had enough chances to roleplay your character’s voice?
3. Which interaction (ally, rival, merchant, faction) felt most engaging?
4. Was any motivation unclear (yours or an NPC’s)? What clarity would help?
5. Name a character bond/flag you want the world to hit more often.
6. Did social stakes feel real? Where could they be raised?
7. Any dialogue beats you’d trim or tighten for momentum?
8. Which faction/organization do you want more screen time with—and how?
9. Did disguises, deception, or persuasion feel fairly adjudicated?
10. What callback to past events would’ve heightened a scene?
1. Which location detail (map, hazard, lore) pulled you in?
2. Did you feel agency in choosing where to go/what to do?
3. Was information discoverable at the right depth (clues, handouts, checks)?
4. Any travel/downtime moment that felt like filler? How to make it pay off?
5. Which mystery/environmental puzzle worked—or needed one more clue?
6. How did resource tracking (time, torches, spell slots) feel—tense or tedious?
7. What worldbuilding thread should we spotlight next session?
8. Did maps/props help you visualize, or do you want a different style?
9. Any procedural step (random encounter, hex, exploration action) to streamline?
10. What secret or vista would make exploration feel more “wow”?
1. What tool (Fantasy Grounds, VTT, dice, initiative method) sped things up?
2. What tool/process slowed us down, and how would you tweak it?
3. Was table time balanced? Anyone need more spotlight or shorter turns?
4. Did audio/music/SFX help or distract? What mix works best?
5. Any house rule to document on a 1-page cheat for quick reference?
6. Were status/effect tracking and conditions clear?
7. Did the recap + goals at start help you focus? What should that include?
8. How was communication (cross-talk, sidebars, clarity)? One fix?
9. Was scheduling/energy right for you? Prefer a break or tighter cadence?
10. What is one quality-of-life change we can try next session?
When harvesting a creature, make an ability check based on its type:

list.li: Nature: Beast, Dragon, Giant, Monstrosity, Plant
Survival: Humanoid
Religion: Celestial, Fiend, Undead
Arcana: Aberration, Construct, Elemental, Fey, Ooze
Harvest DC = 10 + creature CR
Minimum 10, maximum 30

text.p: Success: Harvest all available loot
Failure: Harvest half the loot
Fail by 5 or more: Mishap occurs and all loot is lost
Mishaps may include damaged organs, acid rupture, contamination, or environmental accidents.
A second character can help, granting advantage on the harvesting check.
Some creatures may require proper tools to fully harvest useful parts such as hide, glands, or organs.

list.li: Weapons and armor usually do not require tools
Specialized parts may require Harvester's Tools

text.p: A field kit used for harvesting creature parts.
Includes: bonesaw, thin knife, whetstone, scraper, mincing blade
Cost: 30 gp
During combat, a PC who has not taken their turn this round may swap initiative with another willing PC.

list.li: You may swap initiative only if you have NOT taken your turn yet this round.
You may NOT swap if you have already taken your turn this round.
The new initiative order remains for the rest of the encounter.

text.p: Both players must agree to the swap.
You may drink a healing potion as a Bonus Action or an Action.

list.li: Drink a healing potion as a Bonus Action OR an Action.
Healing is rolled normally either way.
Administering a healing potion to another creature is an Action.
Ground Level (GL): 0–30 ft
LOW: 35–150 ft

text.p: Starting Altitude: 350 ft
Creatures can split movement between horizontal movement (grid) and vertical movement(altitude).
Climb / Dive Rate: Every 5 ft of movement spent = +5 ft (climb) or −5 ft (dive) to altitude.
Movement can be split in any order (move, climb, move, dive, etc.).
A creature that is FALLING drops 100 ft at the end of its turn until it is caught, regains flight, or reaches Ground Level (≤30 ft).
A rider is automatically dismounted if they become:

list.li: Stunned
Unconscious

text.p: Result: The rider instantly drops 100 ft immediately, then becomes FALLING as normal.
A rider must make a DEX save to stay mounted if any of the following occur:

list.li: Grabbed / Grappled / Restrained

text.p: The rider is grabbed, grappled, or otherwise forcibly restrained.

list.li: Critical Hit

text.p: The rider is hit by a critical hit.

list.li: Shoved / Forced Movement

text.p: The rider is shoved or forcibly moved 10 ft or more.

list.li: Heavy Impact Damage

text.p: The rider takes 10+ damage from a single hit/source.

list.li: Mount Takes a Big Hit

text.p: The mount takes 10+ damage from a single hit/source.

list.li: Collision / Obstacle

text.p: The rider or mount collides with an obstacle or hazard impact (debris, cliff face, tornado edge, vortex slam, etc.).

list.li: Knocked Prone While Mounted

text.p: The rider is knocked prone while mounted.

list.li: Mount Incapacitated or Reduced to 0 HP

text.p: If the mount becomes incapacitated or drops to 0 HP, the rider must make the DEX save (DM may rule automatic dismount at 0 HP if desired).
On a failed save: The rider is dismounted → instantly drops 100 ft immediately, then becomes FALLING as normal.
On a successful save: The rider stays mounted.
A catch attempt can be made as a Reaction or Bonus Action .
The catcher must be within 5 ft of the falling creature.
Check: DEX ( Acrobatics ) or WIS ( Animal Handling )
DC 10: same direction (diving with them)
DC 13: crossing angle
DC 16: opposite direction (intercepting while climbing / hard intercept)
Success: the target is caught and no longer FALLING .
Failure: The target continues FALLING as normal.

When a character with the Spellcasting feature finishes a short rest, they recover expended spell slots with a combined level equal to twice their proficiency bonus. No recovered slot can be higher than 5th level.
A character can benefit from this rule once per long rest.

When a character with the Spellcasting feature finishes a short rest, they can recover expended spell slots with a combined level equal to half their proficiency bonus (rounded up). No recovered slot can be higher than 5th level.
A character can use this rule once per long rest.

When a character with the Spellcasting feature finishes a short rest, they can recover expended spell slots with a combined level equal to their proficiency bonus. No recovered slot can be higher than 5th level.
A character can use this feature once per long rest.

text.p: Cryovain the young white dragon is a roaming threat that can be encountered almost anywhere. Each time the characters arrive at a location tagged on the map of the Sword Coast or prepare to leave that location, roll a d20 and consult the Dragon's Location table to determine Cryovain's current whereabouts. Make your first roll on the table when the adventurers leave Phandalin for the first time.

When the dragon visits a location that is not its lair, it surveys the location from the sky, beyond the reach of ranged weapon attacks. If it spots nothing it can eat, it flies off after circling the location for a minute or two. If it spots something tasty, such as a mule, a horse, or a character, the dragon swoops down and attacks it. Once the dragon kills something, it grabs the carcass and flies off with it. Whatever it takes is then eaten within the hour.

If Cryovain loses more than 10 hit points in battle, the dragon disengages from combat and retreats to its lair at Icespire Hold, remaining there until it finishes a long rest and regains all its hit points. Only at Icespire Hold does the dragon fight to the death.

text.frame: “The frontier of Phandalin lies under a gathering shadow. From the peaks of the Sword Mountains, a dragon has descended—its wings scattering beasts, its presence driving monsters into new lairs. With each passing day, the land grows more dangerous. Farms are abandoned, trade routes falter, and rumors of fiery breath and frozen death spread like wildfire. In the wake of this upheaval, the orc tribes have grown restless. Some now march under the guidance of half-orc shamans who gather during stormy nights to perform dark rituals to their storm god. Their rites call down lightning and thunder, and whispers tell of a primal beast loosed upon the plains, thundering across the frontier at their command. Even the dark canopy of Neverwinter Wood is no refuge. When storms roll in, strange lights flicker between the trees, and the cries of unseen things echo through the branches. From the wilds and mountains to the very outskirts of Phandalin itself, danger presses in on all sides. The town has turned to outsiders—adventurers, mercenaries, and would-be heroes. Coin and glory await those bold enough to face the frontier, but so too does a rising storm. This is where your paths cross, and where your story begins.”
text.h: Scene 1: Caravan on the Triboar Trail
text.frame: “The wheels of the caravan creak and groan as it rolls along the rutted Triboar Trail, the late afternoon sun casting long shadows across the fields. To your south, beyond rolling hills, lies the frontier town of Phandalin—the destination of weary travelers, wandering adventurers, and hopeful settlers. Around you, other wagons rumble forward, the sound of hooves and murmured voices carrying in the summer air. This is your moment to introduce yourselves—what do the others see as you travel together toward Phandalin?”

list.li: Let the players roleplay their introductions and reasons for heading to Phandalin.

text.frame: “As the caravan crests a low rise, the driver calls out and turns south onto a smaller trail. There, nestled against the foothills of the Sword Mountains, lies Phandalin—a scattering of stone cottages, wooden homes, and farmland carved from wilderness. It looks quiet, almost peaceful.”

“A sudden, bone-shaking roar splits the air. From the east, the shadow of vast wings sweeps over the trail. A white dragon bursts from the clouds, diving low, its scales flashing like shards of ice in the sunlight. Its cry sends livestock scattering and sets the caravan horses into a panic.” The beast swoops over the wagons, its icy breath blasting across crates of supplies, freezing wood and shattering glass. Livestock scatter into the fields, and settlers scream as the shadow of wings circles overhead. The dragon lashes out at stragglers, tearing into wagons, its tail smashing wood to splinters. If you stand to fight, its wings buffet you, knocking you to the dirt. If you flee, its icy roar chills you to the bone as it hunts the weak and slow. It is a predator, and you are prey.”*
text.p: Cryovain doesn’t fight to kill here—this is a cinematic “you can’t win” encounter:

list.li: Anyone who tries to fight is knocked away by tail swipes, wing gusts, or claws (non-lethal).
Anyone who flees is chased down and eaten by Cryovain—showing the dragon’s lethality without touching PCs.
The caravan leader yells at the PCs to run: “You fools! Run! Get to Phandalin!”

text.frame: “At last, with a triumphant cry, the dragon beats its wings and veers westward, leaving ruin in its wake. The air falls silent, broken only by the sobs of survivors and the panicked whinnies of scattered horses.”

list.li: PCs are forced to run for the safety of the town.
Cryovain doesn’t pursue them directly—he is more interested in terrorizing and feasting on the caravan stragglers.
The party escapes into Phandalin as chaos begins spreading about “the dragon sighting.”

text.frame: “Your lungs burn as you flee the trail, stumbling into the safety of Phandalin. The dragon’s roar fades into the distance, and the townsfolk cautiously emerge from doorways and shutters, faces pale and fearful. Though the dragon doesn’t strike at the town itself, its shadow lingers long in their eyes. A tall, black-scaled dragonborn in a weathered cloak stands in the center of it all, his amber eyes sweeping the scene. You recognize him as the same figure who urged you to run for your lives on the road. He raises a clawed hand and gestures toward the timber-framed inn. ‘Inside, quickly! Rest your feet and your spirits—you’re safe, for now.’”*

list.li: The PCs are guided into Toblen Stonehill’s inn (your image).
Toblen is shaken but hospitable, offering the survivors refuge and a warm hearth.
Immediate Action: He makes sure the party gets inside Stonehill Inn, checks their condition, and reassures them.
Tone: Calm, authoritative, like a veteran who has done this before.
Personality: Uses short, steady phrases to steady the party, mentor-like.

text.frame: “The inn fills with anxious voices. Survivors argue over what remains of the caravan, merchants clutch ledgers in despair, and families sob for those lost on the road. Outside, the streets buzz with fearful talk—the dragon’s roar is on every tongue. The truth is plain: much of the shipment is ruined. Crates of food lie frozen and shattered, health potions scattered in the mud. Without them, miners will suffer, the harvest will falter, and the town’s lifeline is cut thin. ‘The potions were for the mines!’ one merchant cries. ‘Without them, sickness will claim us!’ ‘The fields won’t last without those tools!’ a farmer shouts, fear in his eyes. A caravan guard slams his fist on the table. ‘Half my men are gone, and for what? The dragon’s still out there!’ At last, the dragonborn speaks, his voice steady amid the chaos. He looks to you and says: ‘You saw it with your own eyes. This town won’t last without help. The board will tell you where you’re needed most—but make no mistake. The storm has already broken. Choose your stand.’”

list.li: If the party wanders: Blacktide doesn’t force them; he lets them breathe, but checks in later.
He might approach them in the street or at the inn with a lead: “I heard talk near the Townmaster’s Hall. If you’ve steel enough left in your bones, there’s coin to be had and good you might do.”

p.b: 2. Seeking Quests / Finding the Job Board

list.li: If they find the board first: let the board do the work.
Blacktide will still show up, either confirming what they’ve found or filling in context: “You’ve sharp eyes. Those notices tell half the tale—the rest you’ll hear from the folk who posted them.”

p.b: 3. If They Stall / Don’t Know Where to Go

list.li: Blacktide acts as the gentle nudge, presenting the first quest in-character so momentum never stalls.

text.h: Scene: First Meeting with Kaelen Duskstrider
text.frame: *“The path to Umbrage Hill winds across the open grasslands, the sky heavy with the memory of storms. About an hour into the trek, you hear it: a deep, rumbling roar carried on the wind from the southeast — the very direction of the hill. The sound is primal, shaking the air before fading into uneasy silence. As you steady yourselves, you notice a lone figure crouched by the path ahead. Cloaked in muted green, bow slung across his back, he traces faint impressions in the dirt with gloved fingers. His posture is calm but alert — like a hunter reading the land. When he rises, you see the keen eyes of a wood elf, his gaze sharp as a blade.”*
text.p: If approached peacefully :
Kaelen’s eyes flick to you, lingering a moment before he straightens. His voice is quiet, steady.
text.frame: “Tracks. Something hunts these hills. The roar confirms it.”
text.p: He doesn’t waste words, instead scanning the horizon, always watchful.
text.frame: “I’m following a trail. Someone I seek passed this way. I’ve no time for idle talk — but if your path leads south, perhaps it is the same as mine.”
“I’ve heard worse in the wilds. Whatever it is, it’s hunting. Keep your blades ready.”
text.p: Kaelen narrows his eyes, shoulders his bow, and fades into the tall grass.
text.frame: “Then we’ve nothing to discuss.”
text.p: He retreats immediately, avoiding a fight. If attacked, he disengages and vanishes with the efficiency of a seasoned scout.
Next Scene

linklist.link: Book - D&D Dragon of Icespire Peak

text.p: After initial thanks, Kaelen quietly asks her about his wife:
text.frame: “Wait did this wood elf woman have dark hair, quiet step… she would have spoken her name as Elenya.”

“Yes… I believe I did. She helped me once, with a potion recipe I’d been struggling with. A quiet woman, but clever. She didn’t linger, though — left soon after. Said she was bound for Phandalin I believe she mentioning staying at the Stonehill Inn but that was just a couple days ago.”

list.li: This gives Kaelen his first hopeful lead.

linklist.link: Book - D&D Dragon of Icespire Peak

text.p: Setting: Outside of Phandalin, On a trail
Read-Aloud (Initial Appearance)
text.frame: *“As the road bends around a low ridge, the sound of music drifts toward you — soft strumming, paired with a lilting voice carrying words half-spoken, half-sung. Seated on a boulder beside the trail is a half-elf draped in crimson and gold. His lute rests easily against his thigh as he plays, curls of dark hair catching the sunlight. With a flourish, he strums the final chord and lifts his gaze, his hazel eyes warm and sharp all at once. A smile spreads across his lips, as if your arrival was a cue in a play he’s been rehearsing.”*

“Ah! And here they come — the heroes of this road, wanderers chasing glory or love, or both! Tell me, friends, do you march toward triumph… or tragedy?” He pauses, studying them each with curiosity, as though searching for inspiration for a song.
text.p: Alarion’s gaze lingers on [chosen PC], his smile deepening as if he’s just discovered a verse he’d been missing.
Alarion (to the PC):
text.frame: “Ah… and there you are. The world told me you’d come, though it spoke only in whispers of wind and melody. I could play a thousand songs and none would capture what I see now.” He rises smoothly, bowing with a flourish, one hand over his heart, the other still lightly on his lute. “Forgive me — I speak in riddles when my heart leaps ahead of my head. But I am Alarion, bard, dreamer, and seeker of beauty… and you, stranger, are poetry made flesh.”
“Merely a bard chasing verses, a seeker of beauty on the edge of the wild. I am Alarion — and if you’ll allow it, I’ll make your story mine, and mine yours.”
text.p: If the PC responds warmly :
text.frame: Alarion chuckles, stepping closer. “Then allow me to walk a while with you. Who knows? Perhaps our story is meant to rhyme.”

p.b: If the PC responds coldly or dismissively:

text.frame: He laughs softly, unshaken. “Ah, rejection — as sharp as a dagger, but it sings, too. Even this moment has rhythm. One day, perhaps, you’ll let me finish the verse we’ve begun.”
text.p: If rebuffed:
text.frame: He bows with dramatic grace. “Ah, rejection — the sweetest sting of all! Even this moment has poetry.”
He winks at them. “Jealousy suits you poorly, friend. But fret not — every play needs its chorus as well as its muse.”

list.li: Friendly Response → Alarion asks to walk with them, offering stories, riddles, or even light inspiration.
Neutral / Distrustful → He lingers nearby, humming, jotting notes, sometimes following at a distance.
Hostile → He deflects with humor, refusing to be rattled, then withdraws with a wistful smile.

linklist.link: Book - D&D Dragon of Icespire Peak

text.h: Option 1 — The Inn Performance (Lighthearted, Public Spotlight)
text.p: Setting: Stonehill Inn in Phandalin, evening.
Alarion takes the stage (or simply a table corner) and begins weaving a song about the PCs — but his lyrics lean very heavily toward his chosen “muse.”
The crowd laughs, cheers, or teases the PC in question.
The scene is playful, but the bard’s fixation is clearer now — he might ignore interruptions or double down on the romantic imagery.
Payoff: The party sees him as a flamboyant ally, but also notices his inability to separate “art” from “infatuation.”
text.h: Scene: Alarion at the Stonehill Inn
text.frame: *“The common room of Stonehill Inn is alive with the clatter of mugs and the low hum of conversation. The fire crackles, casting long shadows across the walls. Then the sound of a lute cuts through the din — rich, playful, and perfectly in tune. From atop a table near the hearth, Alarion strums in crimson and gold, his smile bright and unshakable. With a bow to the room, he begins a song that quickly draws the crowd’s attention — and every verse seems to circle back, again and again, to one of you.”*

p.b: Alarion’s Ballad (Directed at the Muse PC)

text.frame: (Sing-song cadence, dramatic pauses) “Oh travelers bold, with hearts of flame, Yet one among them steals the name. A muse of beauty, fierce and true, The gods themselves would bow to you.” (he leans toward the muse PC, eyes never leaving them) “Through storm and night, I’d walk the miles, Just to earn a single smile. Write it down, remember this — The world is poorer without their kiss.”

p.b: If the muse PC responds warmly

text.frame: Alarion flourishes, bowing low, and declares: “And so the verse continues, sweeter than I’d dreamed.”
Alarion smiles wistfully, continuing anyway: “Even the sharpest thorn belongs to the rose — and I’ll still write of its beauty.”

p.b: If another party member heckles him:

text.frame: he spins it into the song: “Ah, jealous hearts, so green they shine — But envy makes a poorer line!”
text.h: Option 2 — The Private Serenade (Intimate, Obsessive Lean)
text.p: Setting: Later that night, the PC he’s fixated on hears faint lute music outside their window or campsite.
Alarion is waiting, playing softly, claiming he “couldn’t sleep until the song was finished.”
He offers them a verse or poem, then confesses:
“I thought I knew beauty. Then I met you, and all I knew crumbled into dust. You are the verse I was born to sing.”
Payoff: Romantic if welcomed, unsettling if not — but either way it cements him as more than just a performer.
text.frame: *“Night settles over Phandalin, quiet but for the murmur of the wind through the eaves. As you settle into rest, a sound drifts through the stillness — soft lute strings, played with aching tenderness. The melody is unmistakable. Outside your window, beneath the pale glow of lanternlight, stands Alarion in crimson and gold. His hazel eyes glimmer as he looks up, his voice rising in song meant only for you.”*

(slow, almost whispered) “The stars may shine, but they are dim, Beside the fire you hold within. The road is long, the night is cold, Yet in your eyes, the dawn takes hold.” (he strums once, softer, and speaks instead of sings) “I thought I knew beauty. Songs, sunsets, painted halls… But they were shadows, echoes, illusions. Then I met you. And every verse I’d ever written crumbled like dust.”
“Forgive me. I should not be here, but the song… it would not let me sleep until I sang it for you. You are the verse I was born to sing, the story I was meant to follow.”
He reaches toward them, but does not touch, hand trembling slightly.
“Tell me only this — do you feel it too? Or shall I be content to be the fool who sings to a closed window?”
He brightens instantly, voice warm. “Then let this be the first verse of many. I will guard it, guard you, with everything I am.”
He bows his head with a soft smile. “Ah… then I shall write my longing into melody and keep it safe, until the day your heart allows me in.”

He freezes, but recovers with a bitter chuckle. “Rejection… sharp as a dagger, yet still a song worth singing. Forgive me, I asked too much. But know this — even if you spurn me, you will always be the verse that haunts my dreams.”
text.h: Option 3 — The Reckless Gesture (Passion Over Tactics)
text.p: Setting: During or right after a dangerous encounter (bandits, orcs, manticores, etc.).
If his “muse” is threatened, Alarion throws himself into reckless action — charging in dramatically, protecting them even if it puts him at serious risk.
After the fight, he downplays the danger:
“What is one life without love to inspire it? I would rather fall than see yours dim, even for a moment.”
Payoff: The party realizes his devotion can be inspiring… or dangerous.
(During Combat)

*“Steel clashes and cries ring out, the fight swirling in chaos. In the midst of it all, Alarion’s gaze snaps to [Muse PC] as a blade or claw strikes dangerously close. His face hardens, the playful mask stripped away. With a cry that’s half-song, half-shout, he charges — strumming his lute with one hand as he hurls himself into the fray, voice booming above the din.”*
text.frame: “Not while I draw breath! Not while the song endures! You’ll not touch them — not my muse, not my heart, not my verse!”
text.p: He positions himself recklessly between the muse PC and the enemy, even if it means leaving his own flank exposed. His magic becomes louder, brighter, more dramatic — as if the battle were a stage, and this, his performance.
If his reckless act succeeds (muse is saved):
text.frame: “You see? What is glory, what is gold, compared to the fire of love? I would fall a thousand times before I’d let harm touch you.”
text.p: If he takes damage for it:
text.frame: “Pain is but another verse in the ballad. And I’ll wear this wound gladly — so long as you still stand.”
text.p: If the muse scolds him for being reckless:
text.frame: “Reckless? Perhaps. But tell me — what would you have me do? Stand by and watch as the world steals you from me?”

linklist.link: Book - D&D Dragon of Icespire Peak

text.h: Scene: First Meeting with Gorvak Stoneheart
text.p: Read Aloud:
text.frame: A jolt. The wagon lurches and groans to a stop. A rear wheel lists at an ugly angle; the oxen snort and stamp in their traces. From the roadside scrub, a broad‑shouldered half‑orc jogs up, hands open. “Easy. I’ve had worse. Let me help.”

list.li: Diagnose: Investigation DC 12 spots a cracked wheel hub and a loosened axle pin.
Calm the team: Animal Handling DC 12 keeps the oxen from panicking (advantage if someone speaks gently and offers feed).
Lift & Brace: Athletics DC 13 to lift the axle while another PC works; with Gorvak assisting, grant advantage.
Repair: Carpenter’s Tools or Tinker’s Tools DC 12 to wedge, pin, and true the wheel. No tools? Improvise with spikes/rope at disadvantage.
Time: 10 minutes on success; on a failed Repair check, add 10 minutes and the next encounter begins mid‑fix.

text.p: Complication (optional, roll 1d4): 1) missing cotter pin (Sleight of Hand DC 12 to fashion one), 2) rain starts (Perception checks at disadvantage until it passes), 3) a crate works loose (Dex save DC 12 or 1 crate damages, –10 gp on payout), 4) an ox’s shoe is loose (Smith’s Tools DC 12 or –2 miles today).
Gorvak’s presence: He automatically Helps the Lift or Repair (DM’s choice). His lines stay short: “Breathe. I’ve got the weight.” “Pin it there… good.”
If the party rudely refuses his help, he backs off but lingers within sight.
A twig snaps. Gorvak’s head turns—then the hiss of arrows from both sides of the trail.

list.li: Surprise: If anyone made Perception DC 13 during the repair (watching the scrub), the party isn’t surprised; otherwise goblins gain advantage on their first volley.
Terrain: Wagon = ½ / ¾ cover; ditches count as difficult terrain; low brush grants lightly obscured.
Tactics: Goblins target driver or beasts first to strand the cargo; they Nimble Escape to break line‑of‑sight after firing.

text.p: A) Dramatic Interpose (light homebrew, recommended for this meet‑cute): 1/scene, when a creature within 5 ft of Gorvak would be reduced to 0 HP by an attack he can see, he uses his Reaction to step in. The attack hits Gorvak instead (same attack roll/damage). If this would drop him to 0, he can stay at 1 HP but suffers 1 level of exhaustion after the fight. Award Inspiration for this sacrifice.

B) RAW-leaning variant: On his turn, Gorvak can Ready: “If an enemy targets an adjacent ally, I move to block, granting them ¾ cover (+5 AC).” If the +5 makes the hit miss, the ally stays up. He can also Shove an ally prone earlier to impose disadvantage on incoming ranged attacks.
After the fight, Gorvak wipes blood from his forearm and checks the wheel. “It’ll hold.”

list.li: RP Toggle: He joins for the rest of the road to Phandalin “to see the wagon safe,” asking no pay.
Check (optional): Persuasion DC 12—on success he commits through delivery; on failure he’ll still shadow the wagon but refuses a formal place.
Benefit: While he travels with them, grant advantage on one more Repair or Animal Handling check on this leg (he anticipates trouble).

text.p: If they let him go: He nods, steps off the trail, and disappears into the brush. Find him later at the Stonehill Inn (evenings).
Stonehill Hook: Children swarm him; the inn comps him a stew. PCs approaching find him humble and direct: “You kept your people upright. That’s the work.”

text.h: Scene: First Encounter with Lyra Shadefoot at the Miner’s Exchange
text.p: Works whether Lyra is not yet with the party (public convo) or already traveling with them (private aside). The “golden statue” is Halia’s euphemism—treat it as any precious relic you prefer; it can be the Conyberry bell re-skinned.
text.h: A) Lyra Not in the Party (Public Convo Stinger)
text.p: Read Aloud:
text.frame: The Exchange floor hums with quiet deals. At the counter, Halia Thornton speaks low to a half-elf woman in a road-scuffed cloak. “—scout it first. Bring me word before anyone else touches it.” The woman flips a coin and smirks. “A golden statue, huh? Sounds like a trinket.” Halia’s gaze doesn’t blink. “It’s not. You’ll do it.” A reluctant shrug. “Fine. I’ll look.” The woman pockets the coin, turns past you with a breeze of wildflower soap and ink, and slips out into town.

list.li: Perception DC 13 (as they cross the floor): Catch the phrase “golden statue” and “scout first.”
Insight DC 12: Note strain—Lyra is dismissive, but obligated.
Insight DC 14: Halia’s tone has leverage—this isn’t a casual favor.
If asked now: Halia sidesteps (see “Deflection,” below).

p.b: Where Lyra goes: She lingers near the Shrine of Luck (bench under the eaves).

list.li: Approach Lyra (soft): She’s wry but cagey. “Just a favor for a friend. Don’t make a hymn of it.”
Persuasion DC 12: She admits it’s a scouting job; no details.
Persuasion DC 15 or a concrete favor offered (e.g., share road intel): She hints it’s north*east of town and not to ring anything you don’t understand.
Pushy tactics (Intimidation DC 14): She smiles thinly, gives nothing, ends the convo. Future DCs with her +1 until mended.
Follow/Shadow to the shrine: Stealth vs Lyra’s Passive Perception 14. If spotted, she waves you over instead of escalating.
Deception +5 vs Insight: “Supply work. A marker statue for a boundary dispute—nothing that delays your contract.”
Counterplay: Produce a bribe of info (e.g., bandit sign, storm front) → she thanks you but still stonewalls.
If PCs parley smartly (Persuasion DC 15): She offers a minor sweetener on the supply run (+10 gp in goods) but keeps the statue job separate.

text.p: Recruitment Beat (optional): After the shrine chat, Lyra can be hired as a scout-on-retainer (1 day only) for 5 gp; she provides advantage on the next Navigation/Watch check.
text.h: B) Lyra Already in the Party (Private Aside)
text.frame: As business wraps, Halia’s eyes flick to Lyra. “A word.” She leads her three steps aside, voices low. The room hushes around coin and parchment.

list.li: Perception DC 15 (line-of-sight, casual): Catch fragments—“golden statue… scout first… report to me.”
Stealth DC 13 to drift closer without drawing Halia’s gaze; then Perception DC 12 to hear more.
If spotted: Halia re-angles, ends the talk: “Later, Ms. Shadefoot.”
Asking Lyra openly: She keeps it short. “Doing her a favor. Won’t slow us down.”
Insight DC 13: She’s hiding who benefits and how soon she intends to peel off.
Persuasion DC 15 plus an offered boundary (e.g., “we’ll choose if we split, not you alone”): She agrees to report to the group first if the lead surfaces this session.
Ultimatums push her quiet and brittle; future trust checks +1 DC with her.

text.p: Halia’s Tone (private): Crisp, clinical. “Scout it first. No fingerprints. Tell me, not the tavern.”

list.li: If the PCs approach Lyra at the shrine respectfully, Sister Garaele offers a nod and tea.
Religion or Insight DC 10: Sense that Lyra’s mask is thinner here.
If the party shows mercy/aid elsewhere in town, Garaele later vouches for them to Lyra (reduce future social DCs with Lyra by 2 once).
Keep it casual: Lyra remains a friendly contact; she’ll share a travel tip next time they leave town (advantage on one random encounter check).
Hire her briefly: She scouts a watch at dusk and points out bandit sign (grant advantage to avoid ambush once).
Alienate her: If bullied, she goes cool; subtract one future chance to steer her away from Zhent orders.

linklist.link: Book - D&D Dragon of Icespire Peak

text.h: Scene: Meeting Selene Vaelor en route to Dwarven Excavation
text.frame: *“The rocky trail twists into the foothills, the land scarred by old mining roads and broken stone. Ahead, you spot a figure standing with a heavy tome in her hands, muttering under her breath as she turns slowly in place. Maps and loose parchment flap in the wind from a satchel at her side, and the silver runes on her sapphire-blue robes catch the fading light. She glances up, her expression composed but uncertain, and you realize she has been circling the same bend in the path for some time.”
“Ah — forgive me, but perhaps you know the way? I was certain the dwarven excavation was near this ridge, yet my maps… well, they seem to disagree with the terrain.”
text.p: She smiles faintly, relieved.
text.frame: “I knew I should have trusted my instincts rather than my notes. Your company would be most welcome — I’ve no desire to stumble into another circle of the same hills.”

p.b: If the party teases her (book-smart but lost):

text.p: She sighs but chuckles softly.
text.frame: “Yes, I suppose maps are far less reliable than roads under one’s feet. A lesson I am learning repeatedly.”

p.b: If the party is hostile or dismissive:

text.p: She stiffens with quiet dignity.
text.frame: “Very well. Then I shall persist on my own. But know that knowledge is best shared, not hoarded.”
text.p: If they leave her behind, she may still appear later at the excavation, having found her way eventually.

linklist.link: Book - D&D Dragon of Icespire Peak

text.h: Scene: Selene’s Reaction to the Staff Fragment
text.frame: As the dust settles and the jelly’s remains hiss into stillness, Selene steps forward. Her eyes catch on the staff fragment lying atop the bloodstained altar. For a heartbeat she stares, lips parted, the mask of calm scholarship slipping. She reaches for it with trembling hands, tracing the faint Elvish inscription — “Vaelor.” Selene (voice trembling with excitement): “At last… my studies, all these years… it wasn’t folly. This is real. A piece of the Staff of Vaelor.” She presses the fragment close, her composure breaking into a rare smile. “But this is only part of it. The rest must be out there. Somewhere. I’ll need time — research, maps, old records… but if one fragment endured here, then the others are within reach.”
text.h: If the Party Asks About It
text.p: Her composure hardens, her voice returning to its usual calm, measured cadence:
Selene (distant, reserved):
text.frame: “It’s nothing of consequence to you. An heirloom… my family’s name is carved into it. That is all.”
She slips it into her satchel, gaze lowering as if closing a door.
“I’ll see to it it’s kept safe. The ruins still hold dangers more pressing than this.”

text.h: Scene: First Meeting with Tobin “Tobble” Reedfellow
text.frame: A soot-kissed halfling in a bulging tool-satchel pops into [location/scene], hair slightly singed and eyes bright. A brass cricket-gadget in his hand [clicks / hums / chirps] whenever it points at [nearby material/object]. “Name’s Tobble—artificer, volunteer optimist. There’s trouble in Gnomegarde—something pretending to be [tools / furniture / gear]. If you’ve got ropes and a calm hand, we can fix this before it gets worse.”

p.b: If the party presses for details (pick one):Tobble shares a quick field-testing protocol and lends gear.

list.li: Protocol (non-destructive): dust with flour to map edges; side-tap resonance test (ring vs thunk); check heat/ozone near mechanisms; light-angle and mirror tests for glamours; simple call-and-response to spot scripted behavior.
Gear: Form-Finder Cricket (once/short rest: advantage on one Investigation to reveal a disguised object within 10 ft), chalk symbols gnomes recognize, fine oil for brighter lantern work.
Goal: “Document the phenomenon, learn its tells, and help the gnomes stop more from vanishing.”

text.frame: “Yes! I’ll keep behind the pointy bits—observe, test, take notes. If something’s odd, I’ll say odd very loudly.”
text.p: Quick mechanics (optional):

list.li: Tobble’s Aid: Once per room/area, Tobble uses the Help action to grant advantage to one Investigation or Arcana check aimed at identifying a strange object/mechanism.
Nervous Tinkerer: If combat starts within 10 ft of Tobble, he automatically Dashes to cover on his first turn.

text.p: What he brings: Form-Finder Cricket (once/short rest: adv. on one Investigation to reveal a disguised object within 10 ft), chalk symbols gnomes recognize, fine lamp oil.
Follow-on beat: He starts a field log, asking PCs to call out anything that “rings vs. thunks.”

p.b: If they leave him be (ask him to stay in town)

text.frame: “Prudent. I’ll prep reference notes and wait at the Stonehill. Bring me anything puzzling—I’ll diagram it.”

list.li: Research Note: You depart with a stamped card from Tobble. On arrival at Gnomengarde, your first parley check starts at +1 Trust (they recognize his mark).
Off-screen Analyst: If you return with an unidentified device, Tobble can Identify it with Arcana DC 12 (or 10 minutes of study), giving you a clear description and safe-use steps.

text.p: What he leaves you: Chalk bundle, simple test list (flour dust, side-tap, mirror check).
Follow-on beat: If the party is delayed 2+ long rests, Tobble sends a runner with rumor updates or a sketched map addition (you choose).

p.b: If they reject him (decline brusquely or bar him)

text.frame: “Right. I’ll… step aside. If you learn anything, please—leave word. I have to understand what’s happening to them.”

list.li: Keep Him from Going Solo: Persuasion DC 12—on success he promises to stay put; on failure he’ll try to hire a guide and head out after 1 long rest (you may meet him en route or find signs he passed through).
Fewer Clues: Without Tobble’s kit, the party loses the once/short-rest Cricket advantage (unless they already have it).

text.p: What he still shares (polite rejection): A brief route note (“follow the southeast stream; spoon-chimes mark their approach”).
Follow-on beat: If he goes on his own, set a soft clock: after 2 long rests, word reaches Phandalin that “a halfling tinkerer” was seen near the gnome caves—possible rescue or complication hook.
